name: Sunifiram
lead: Sunifiram (DM-235) is an experimental nootropic from a series of piperazine compounds made by Italian researchers; it is a structural simplification of unifiram (DM-232). In animal studies it showed antiamnesic effects at much lower doses than piracetam.[1][2] It has not been approved anywhere.[3]

It reaches appearance-minded communities indirectly. Forum users who train and diet for physique goals sometimes discuss nootropic stacks for focus and drive in the gym or at work, and sunifiram appears in a few such posts alongside racetams.[7][8] Nothing in the research literature links it to physical appearance; the interest is in cognition and motivation, which proponents see as supporting consistent training, studying and self-improvement.

The compound was disclosed in the early 2000s by an academic group in Florence and left unpatented, and about twelve years later its originator found dozens of websites selling it as a cognitive enhancer for healthy people even though only a few preclinical studies had been done and its long-term toxicity was unknown.[3] As of 2016 it had undergone no toxicology testing and no human trials.[1][3]
infobox: Unapproved new drug in the US; not approved anywhere[1][3]

paras: Sunifiram is 1-benzoyl-4-propanoylpiperazine, a benzamide and N-benzoylpiperazine derivative (CAS 314728-85-3). It is a simplified version of unifiram, and another analogue is sapunifiram (MN-19).[1] Wikipedia points to a 2000 Journal of Medicinal Chemistry paper on 'molecular simplification' of related compounds as part of the chemical background.[1] Grokipedia describes it as structurally related to piracetam in function though built on a piperazine rather than pyrrolidone ring, and as a white to off-white crystalline powder made by acylation of piperazine.[9]

The mechanism is unknown. Broad screening found no affinity for tested receptors, ion channels and transporters up to 1 micromolar, and it did not potentiate AMPA receptors directly, though it blocked amnesia from an AMPA antagonist.[1][4] A 2003 study reported that AMPA receptor activation is involved in the antiamnesic effects of unifiram and sunifiram.[10] Later mouse and hippocampal work linked it to the NMDA receptor glycine site and to CaMKII and PKC activation, with enhanced hippocampal synaptic efficacy in slice experiments.[5][6]

Reviews also report increased acetylcholine release from rat cortical slices, and Wikipedia notes inhibition of barbiturate- and diazepam-related inhibition of glucose transport in human erythrocytes in vitro, considered unlikely to be the main mechanism.[1][4]

In mice, sunifiram prevented scopolamine-induced amnesia in a passive-avoidance task at doses far lower than piracetam or aniracetam, with an effect described as comparable to those drugs at much larger doses.[2] The 2006 review described unifiram and sunifiram as four orders of magnitude more potent than piracetam in these models.[4] In olfactory bulbectomized mice, sunifiram improved cognitive deficits via CaM kinase II and protein kinase C activation.[6]

The unifiram family emerged from the University of Florence's work on piracetam-related cognition enhancers, with structure-activity studies of DM232 and DM235 published in 2004 and analogue design continuing in 2008 and 2009.[2][11][12] The originator later wrote that the compounds were not protected by a patent for a variety of reasons, which left them free for anyone to sell once disclosed.[3] A 2022 paper on sunifiram-carbamate hybrids was later retracted.[13]

The word nootropic was coined by Corneliu Giurgea in 1972 for substances said to improve learning and memory without fitting existing drug categories. Wikipedia notes there is no globally accepted clinical definition and that most compounds sold under the label do not meet his criteria.[14]

Sunifiram is described by its originators as a piracetam-related compound, and the racetams (piracetam, aniracetam, oxiracetam) are the best-known family it is compared with. Wikipedia reports that racetams have few serious side effects but little evidence of enhancing cognition in people without impairment, and that piracetam and aniracetam are positive modulators of AMPA receptors, although their mechanisms are poorly understood.[14]

In 2019 the FDA and FTC warned manufacturers and consumers about deceptive advertising of nootropics, and Wikipedia notes that products marketed as supplements but containing unapproved drugs are illegal in the United States. A 2019 study found piracetam supplements inaccurately labelled.[14]
No studies found. A 2016 review in the Journal of Enzyme Inhibition and Medicinal Chemistry discussed how the compounds reached online markets without human data.[3]

The compound is not patented and is sold online as a research chemical or nootropic.[3] In the US it is an unapproved new drug, and Wikipedia states that use in dietary supplements, food or medicine is unlawful.[1] No adverse-effect data exist because toxicology has not been studied.[1][3]

On T Nation, sunifiram appears occasionally in users' personal stacks, for example in a long thread on symptoms of low testosterone where a poster described moving from piracetam to stronger racetams and sunifiram, and in a trip report listing substances the writer had tried.[7][8]

lore.intro: Sunifiram is mentioned in nootropic and physique forum threads as one ingredient in personal stacks, usually without systematic reporting.[7][8]

claims.claim: Sunifiram is a far more potent nootropic than piracetam
claims.believers: Posters describe stacking it with racetams to maintain a cognitive effect they felt faded over time.[7]
claims.experts: Animal studies report antiamnesic effects at doses far below piracetam's; no human trials exist.[2][3][4]

claims.claim: Sunifiram is safe because it is used at low amounts
claims.believers: Online sellers market it as a cognitive enhancer for healthy people.[3]
claims.experts: The originating researcher wrote that long-term toxicity was unknown and that no toxicology testing or human trials had been done as of 2016.[3]

card.summary: An unapproved animal-tested nootropic with no human trials and no appearance evidence.
card.note: No human trials or toxicology testing.

quick.overview:
Sunifiram is an experimental nootropic developed in Italy and sold online. It is a simplified analogue of unifiram.

No source links it to appearance.
quick.mechanism: Its mechanism is unknown; research points to NMDA glycine-site and kinase pathways.
quick.risks: No human trials or toxicology testing have been published; unapproved in the US.

chain: Proposed to boost NMDA/AMPA-related synaptic signalling in the hippocampus
More consistent training and study habits supporting self-improvement
angle.text: People who take nootropics describe wanting better focus and motivation to keep up demanding training or study routines. Sunifiram's reputation rests on animal studies of memory and on user reports; no human trial has tested it for any outcome, including appearance.
